title: 話す → 話せる
titleEn: Can do: the potential form (〜える, 〜られる, できる)
summary: To say you can do something, change the verb: 話す → 話せる, 食べる → 食べられる, する → できる. The result describes what's possible, not an action, so what you can do usually takes が.
explanation: English adds a word ("can"). Japanese **changes the verb itself**. {話|はな}す (speak) becomes {話|はな}せる (be able to speak). The new verb is an ordinary る-verb, so it takes ます like any other: {話|はな}せます, {話|はな}せません.

**う-verbs: change the last -u to -e and add る.** {話|はな}す → {話|はな}せる, {行|い}く → {行|い}ける, {泳|およ}ぐ → {泳|およ}げる, {買|か}う → {買|か}える, {作|つく}る → {作|つく}れる, {歩|ある}く → {歩|ある}ける. **る-verbs: drop る, add られる.** {食|た}べる → {食|た}べられる, {見|み}る → {見|み}られる, {出|で}かける → {出|で}かけられる. **The two odd ones: する → できる, {来|く}る → {来|こ}られる.** Note the reading: こられる, not きられる.

**A potential verb describes a state, not an action.** {話|はな}せる doesn't say you're doing anything. It says what's possible for you. That's why it acts like the "it happens" verbs from Lesson 4: the thing you can do usually takes **が**. {日本語|にほんご}**を**{話|はな}します = I speak Japanese (an action). {日本語|にほんご}**が**{話|はな}せます = Japanese is something I can speak. You'll also hear を with potential verbs, especially in longer sentences. Both are fine, but が is the one to aim for.

**できる is the workhorse.** Any する-verb turns into "can" by swapping する for できる: {練習|れんしゅう}する → {練習|れんしゅう}できる, {録音|ろくおん}する → {録音|ろくおん}できる. On a trip, **〜できますか** (can I…?) opens more doors than any other question.

**Some verbs already mean "can".** {分|わ}かる (understand), {見|み}える (be visible) and {聞|き}こえる (be audible) are about something reaching you, so they have no potential form. Keep {見|み}える and {見|み}られる apart: {見|み}える = it's in view, on its own. {見|み}られる = you're able to see it, because it's on show or you get the chance. From your room the sea {見|み}えます. At a museum, old photos {見|み}られます.
**In casual speech the ら drops:** {見|み}れる, {食|た}べれる, {来|こ}れる. You'll hear these everywhere, from friends and on TV, so don't let them throw you. In your own polite sentences, use the full form.
Why it matters for you: "Can I…?" and "I can… a little" are how you start talking with someone. **{日本語|にほんご}が{少|すこ}し{話|はな}せます** tells a stranger at the bar that they can talk to you.

examples.ja: {日本語|にほんご}が{少|すこ}し{話|はな}せます。
examples.en: I can speak a little Japanese.
examples.note: 話す → 話せる. が for what you can do.

examples.ja: カードは{使|つか}えますか。
examples.note: 使う → 使える. は because you're asking about cards as opposed to cash.

examples.ja: {生|なま}の{魚|さかな}も{食|た}べられます。
examples.en: I can eat raw fish too.
examples.note: A る-verb: 食べる → 食べられる. Worth having ready at any dinner table.

examples.ja: ここで{録音|ろくおん}できますか。
examples.note: 録音する → 録音できる. で marks where the recording happens (Lesson 2).

examples.ja: {窓|まど}から{山|やま}が{見|み}えます。
examples.en: You can see the mountains from the window.
examples.note: 見える is its own verb (be visible), not the potential of 見る.

examples.ja: すみません、{明日|あした}は{出|で}かけられません。
examples.en: Sorry, I can't go out tomorrow.
examples.note: 出かける is a る-verb, so 出かけられる. Negative: 出かけられません.

a.ja: {日本語|にほんご}を{話|はな}します。

b.ja: {日本語|にほんご}が{話|はな}せます。

contrasts.why: 話します is an action, so the thing you speak takes を. 話せます is a state (what's possible for you), so the default is が.

a.ja: {窓|まど}から{山|やま}が{見|み}えます。
a.en: The mountains are visible from the window.

b.ja: ここで{古|ふる}い{写真|しゃしん}が{見|み}られます。
b.en: You can see old photos here.

contrasts.why: 見える: the view reaches your eyes on its own. 見られる: you're able to look because the photos are on show here. One is about the view, the other about the chance to see it.

a.ja: ここで{練習|れんしゅう}しますか。

b.ja: ここで{練習|れんしゅう}できますか。

contrasts.why: します asks about the plan. できます asks whether it's possible or allowed. Use the second one when you need permission for the room.

exercises.scene: At a counter bar, the person next to you asks: 日本語、話せますか。
exercises.en: Yes, I can speak a little.

options.why: They asked 話せますか (can you?), so answer with the potential: 話す → 話せる → 話せます.
少し話します = I do speak a little, as an activity. People will understand you, but it answers "do you?" rather than "can you?".
話される is the passive ("gets spoken"). For a う-verb the potential is just -e + る: 話せる.

exercises.scene: Your host is planning the menu.

options.why: 食べる is a る-verb: drop る, add られる → 食べられる.
生の魚は食べますか = do you eat raw fish? A question about habit, not ability. Close, but the host wants to know whether you can.
Not a form. Only う-verbs change -u to -e. る-verbs add られる.

exercises.scene: You'd like to record in the studio tonight.
exercises.prompt: {今夜|こんや}、スタジオで{録音|ろくおん}＿＿か。
exercises.en: Can I record in the studio tonight?

options.why: する-verbs swap する for できる: 録音する → 録音できる.
録音しますか = are you recording? / will you record? It asks about a plan, not whether it's possible.
される is the passive of する ("gets recorded"). The potential of する is できる.

exercises.scene: Describing your room at the inn.
exercises.prompt: {部屋|へや}の{窓|まど}から{海|うみ}が＿＿。
exercises.en: You can see the sea from the room's window.

options.why: The sea just comes into view on its own: 見える, with が.
Not wrong, but it frames the view as an opportunity on offer, like a hotel brochure. To say the sea is simply in view, 見えます.
見せる = show someone. The sea isn't showing anything to anyone.

exercises.prompt: {日本語|にほんご}＿{少|すこ}し{話|はな}せます。
exercises.en: I can speak a little Japanese.

options.why: With a potential verb, what you can do is the subject of the state: 日本語が話せます.
日本語で話せます = I can talk in Japanese (Japanese as the means, Lesson 2). Grammatical, but it means "we can have this conversation in Japanese", not "I have some Japanese".
に marks a point (where something is or where it arrives). Japanese isn't a destination here.

exercises.prompt: {明日|あした}は{何時|なんじ}に＿＿か。
exercises.en: What time can you come tomorrow?

options.why: 来る is irregular: its potential is 来られる, read こられる.
The kanji is right but the reading isn't. The potential of 来る is こられる.
くれる is a different verb: give (to me). 何時にくれますか = what time will you give it to me?

exercises.scene: Your pickup asks if you need a ride.
exercises.prompt: {大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}です。{一人|ひとり}で{駅|えき}まで＿＿。
exercises.en: It's fine. I can walk to the station on my own.

options.why: 歩く is a う-verb: -ku → -ke + る → 歩ける → 歩けます.
一人で駅まで歩きます = I'll walk to the station myself. Fine as a plan, but it doesn't say you're able to.
歩かれる is the passive or honorific form, not "can walk".

exercises.scene: A friend invites you out. Say you can't go out tomorrow.
exercises.why: 出かける is a る-verb: 出かけられる, negative 出かけられません. 出かけません would mean you won't go out, which sounds like a choice.

exercises.scene: At the register, ask if you can pay by card.
exercises.why: 使う → 使える (-u → -e + る). 使いますか would ask whether they use cards, not whether you can.

exercises.scene: Your exhibition opening. Someone starts talking to you in fast Japanese. Say you can speak a little Japanese and ask them to speak slowly.
exercises.model: {日本語|にほんご}が{少|すこ}し{話|はな}せます。ゆっくり{話|はな}してください。
exercises.en: I can speak a little Japanese. Please speak slowly.
exercises.why: 話せます (potential, with が) tells them you have some Japanese; 話してください is the ordinary request form of 話す.
